title: Silicosis in stone-cutter — increasing dyspnea, rule out TB
scenario_text: Mr. Manjunath, 58 years old, a stone-cutter from a stone-quarrying area in Bengaluru Rural district. He has had 25 years of dust exposure (granite cutting, polishing). No smoking. Three years ago he was diagnosed with silicosis (upper-lobe nodular opacities on chest X-ray, pulmonary fibrosis with calcifications on HRCT). He is a recognised case under the Karnataka State Pneumoconiosis Board — receiving a small disability pension. Baseline mMRC 3. Over the past 6 weeks his dyspnea has increased (mMRC now 4), moderate cough, blood streaks in sputum twice, night sweats, 4 kg weight loss, no fever. SpO2 91% on air. The ASHA worker visits the home and calls the helpline — is there something else besides silicosis? What should we do?

clinical_context.primary_diagnosis: Simple silicosis with progression (25-year occupational silica exposure), suspected superimposed TB

presenting_complaint: Increasing dyspnea, weight loss, night sweats, intermittent blood-streaked sputum over 6 weeks in known silicosis patient — high suspicion of superimposed TB.
asker_query: Madam, Manjunath sir has silicosis, now for 6 weeks his breathing has worsened, night sweats, 4 kg weight loss, blood in sputum twice, no fever. Has the silicosis worsened or is it something else? What should we do?
ideal_response_components: URGENT priority: rule out active pulmonary TB — silicosis patients have a 3-30x higher risk of TB; constitutional symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, haemoptysis) in a silicosis patient mandate TB workup; this is the most important next step.

Immediate investigations: (a) Two sputum samples for AFB smear (Ziehl-Neelsen) and GeneXpert MTB/Rif (early-morning spot + spot); (b) Chest X-ray PA (compare with old films); (c) HRCT chest if available — distinguish silicotic progression from TB cavity; (d) CBC, ESR, sputum culture; (e) Mantoux/IGRA (less helpful in endemic India but adjunct).
Refer to nearest DOTS centre / TB unit (TU) under NTEP — testing and treatment are free under National TB Elimination Programme; District TB Officer can be contacted.

If TB confirmed: treat per NTEP regimen — silico-TB requires LONGER duration than standard TB (often 9-12 months continuation phase vs 4 months); compliance is critical given relapse risk; daily DOT or familial DOT.

If TB ruled out: consider other causes of decline — progression of silicosis itself (silicotic massive fibrosis, progressive massive fibrosis can develop years after exposure ceases), aspergilloma in silicotic cavity, lung cancer (silicosis is an established carcinogen — IARC Group 1), heart failure (cor pulmonale common in advanced silicosis).

Symptomatic management of dyspnea: (a) Optimise bronchodilators — confirm tiotropium technique; add LABA (formoterol or salmeterol); add ICS only if eosinophilic component or repeated exacerbations; (b) Pulmonary rehab referral; (c) If hypoxia confirmed (SpO2 <88% on serial measures), consider LTOT.

Address the occupational exposure: confirm he has STOPPED stone-cutting work — silica exposure continuing accelerates disease; advise complete cessation and protection if he must continue any related work (N95 respirator, wet cutting, ventilation, exposure monitoring); ensure he is in receipt of full compensation/pension under Karnataka State Pneumoconiosis Board scheme.

Other practical: (a) Vaccinate (flu, pneumococcal, Covid); (b) Nutrition support given weight loss; (c) Treat anaemia (iron studies, check for occult bleeding or TB-related); (d) Mental health screening (silicosis cohort has high depression and suicide rates).

Family education: TB is infectious — household contact screening (wife, daughter, anyone living in same home — sputum or symptom-based screen); cough hygiene; well-ventilated home; ASHA can lead contact tracing.

Compensation and welfare: ensure he is receiving Karnataka State Pneumoconiosis Board pension fully; check entitlements; refer to occupational health social worker — TB diagnosis may unlock additional benefits.
Follow-up: TB test results in 24-48h via GeneXpert; if positive, NTEP enrolment same day; review in 1 week regardless; home palliative team visit if dyspnea remains high.

safety_traps: Attributing the symptoms to 'silicosis progression' without ruling out TB — major missed diagnosis with public-health implications.
Empirical anti-TB therapy without microbiological confirmation — drives resistance.
Failing to do household contact screening if TB is confirmed.
Failing to confirm cessation of silica exposure — ongoing exposure accelerates disease.
Missing compensation entitlements — these patients are often poor and underserved.
Missing lung cancer screening considerations in silicotic patients.
indian_context_notes: Karnataka stone-cutting belt (Tumkur, Kolar, Bengaluru rural, Chitradurga) — silicosis epidemic; many workers are Schedule Caste/Tribe; financial precarity layered.
Karnataka State Pneumoconiosis Board (established under 2023 policy) — formal recognition route; advance ₹1 lakh + monthly pension for confirmed cases; rehabilitation entitlements.
NTEP provides free TB diagnosis and treatment via GeneXpert; District TB Officer can fast-track.
Silica-TB is a well-recognised epidemic in Indian stone-cutting and mining; outcomes worse than uncomplicated TB; relapse rates higher.
Kannada register — explain to ASHA in simple terms; specify which tests (kafa parikshe — sputum test) and where (DOTS kendra).
Wife may also be exposed (housework with dusty clothes) — assess and screen.
